seo_title: Insurance Loss Reported Meaning: What It Means for You
meta_description: Insurance loss reported meaning explained: what the phrase means on claims, CLUE reports and car history reports, and what happens after you report a loss.
h1: Insurance Loss Reported Meaning: What It Is and Why It Matters

excerpt: What does insurance loss reported mean? Learn what the phrase means on your claim, on CLUE loss history reports and on vehicle history reports, plus what happens next.
key_takeaways: Insurance loss reported means the insurer was formally notified of a possible covered loss.
The phrase also appears on CLUE property reports and vehicle history reports.
You can request a free CLUE report each year and dispute errors.
Texas carriers generally must acknowledge a claim within 15 days of notice.
Report promptly, document thoroughly and review the carrier's estimate line by line.
body_html:
"Insurance loss reported" means a policyholder formally notified an insurance company about damage, theft or another loss that may be covered by a policy. The report opens a claim file and starts the insurer's investigation. The phrase also appears on loss history and vehicle history reports to show a claim was filed on that property or car.

What does insurance loss reported mean?

In plain English, an insurance loss reported is a loss the insurer has officially been told about. You call, file online or submit a written notice saying something happened, such as hail on your roof, a kitchen fire or a burst pipe, and the carrier records it. From that moment, there is a record that a loss was reported, even before anyone decides whether it is covered or how much it is worth.

You will see the phrase in three main places:

  • On your own claim: the carrier's acknowledgment letter or portal may show a status like "loss reported" while the file is being opened and assigned.
  • On a property loss history report: databases insurers share list past reported losses on a home or policyholder.
  • On a vehicle history report: "insurance loss reported" or "total loss reported" tells a buyer an insurer handled a claim on that car.

Insurance loss reported vs claim filed

People use the two phrases interchangeably, and in most cases they describe the same event. Technically, a loss is reported when you notify the carrier, and a claim is the formal request for payment that the carrier opens and processes. Some carriers record a reported loss first and then convert it to a claim once coverage information is confirmed.

The distinction matters for two reasons. First, the date you report the loss is the date that usually starts the insurer's response deadlines in Texas. Second, a reported loss can appear on your loss history even if you later decide not to pursue the claim. If you are unsure whether damage is worth a claim, ask a contractor or estimator to look at it before you call, but do not delay so long that notice becomes late.

Reporting a loss is not the same as getting paid. It is the first step, and how well that first step is handled affects everything that follows.

What is an insurance loss?

An insurance loss is any damage, destruction or financial harm that may trigger payment under a policy. For property owners, that usually means physical damage to a building or its contents. For insurers, "loss" also refers to the dollar amount they pay out on claims.

Common types of reported losses

Type of lossExamplesTypical coverage
WeatherHail, wind, tornado, lightning, iceHomeowners or commercial property policy
Fire and smokeKitchen fires, electrical fires, wildfireHomeowners or commercial property policy
WaterBurst pipes, appliance leaks, roof leaks after stormsCovered if sudden and accidental; flood requires separate coverage
Theft and vandalismBreak-ins, stolen property, malicious damageHomeowners, renters or commercial policy
LiabilityA visitor injured on your propertyLiability section of the policy
AutoCollisions, hail on vehicles, theftAuto policy (collision or comprehensive)

In Texas, weather is the big one. Hail across Dallas-Fort Worth, Central Texas and the Panhandle, plus hurricanes along the Gulf Coast, drive a large share of property losses reported each year.

What is an insurance loss report?

An insurance loss report, sometimes called a loss run or loss history report, is a record of claims reported on a property, a person or a vehicle. It is different from the notice you give your carrier. The notice starts one claim. The loss report summarizes your claim history.

A typical property loss report includes:

  • The date of loss and the date it was reported
  • The type or cause of loss, such as wind, hail, water or fire
  • The property address and policy information
  • Claim status, such as open, closed, paid or closed without payment
  • The amount paid, if any

The CLUE report

For homes and autos, the best-known database is the Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (CLUE), maintained by LexisNexis. Participating insurers contribute claim information, and underwriters check it when you apply for a new policy or buy a home. Records generally cover about the last seven years.

Under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, you are entitled to a free copy of your consumer report from these databases once a year, and you can dispute information that is inaccurate. Homebuyers can also ask a seller for a CLUE report on the home before closing.

Tip: Review your CLUE report before you shop for insurance or sell your home. Correcting an error early is far easier than explaining it to an underwriter later.

What is insurance loss reported on a car?

On a vehicle history report, "insurance loss reported" means an insurer paid or handled a claim involving that vehicle. It could be a minor hail claim, a collision repair or a total loss. The entry alone does not tell you how serious the damage was.

  • Insurance loss reported: a claim was filed and recorded; check the details for severity.
  • Total loss reported: the insurer decided repair costs were too high relative to the car's value and paid it off as a total loss.
  • Salvage or rebuilt title: a title brand that often follows a total loss.

If you are buying a used car with a reported loss, ask for repair records and get an independent inspection. A reported hail loss on a Texas car, for instance, may be minor cosmetic denting or may involve significant panel and glass replacement.

Why does reporting a loss quickly matter?

Nearly every property policy requires "prompt" notice of a loss. Reporting quickly protects your claim in several ways:

  1. It preserves evidence. Hail marks, water stains and fire residue change over time. Fresh damage is easier to tie to a specific event.
  2. It meets policy conditions. Late notice gives the carrier an argument that it was harmed by the delay.
  3. It starts Texas claim deadlines. Under the Prompt Payment of Claims Act (Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542), insurers generally must acknowledge a claim within 15 days of notice, then accept or reject it within 15 business days of receiving the items they requested.
  4. It limits further damage. Reporting early gets mitigation and temporary repairs moving and documented.

Our Texas claim deadline calculator shows how those timelines play out from the date you report. For a fuller explanation of the notice itself, see our guide to the notice of loss insurance definition. This is general information, not legal advice.

How to report an insurance loss the right way

A clear first report sets up a smoother claim. Before you call, gather the basics.

  1. Make the property safe and take reasonable steps to prevent more damage. Keep receipts for tarps, water extraction and board-up.
  2. Photograph and video everything before cleanup, including wide shots and close-ups with the date visible if possible.
  3. Write down the facts: date, time, cause and what you saw. Stick to what you know and avoid guessing about cause or age of damage.
  4. Contact your insurer by phone, app or online portal, and get a claim number.
  5. Follow up in writing with a short email confirming what you reported and when.
  6. Keep a claim log of every call, email and inspection.

Our free claim documentation checklist walks through the photos, receipts and records worth keeping.

What happens after a loss is reported?

StageWhat happens
Claim openedThe insurer assigns a claim number and an adjuster.
AcknowledgmentTexas carriers generally must acknowledge the claim and request needed information within 15 days.
InspectionAn adjuster or inspector documents the damage, often with photos and measurements.
EstimateThe carrier writes a repair estimate, typically in Xactimate or Symbility.
DecisionThe insurer accepts, partially accepts or denies the claim.
PaymentOnce accepted, payment generally follows within 5 business days, minus deductible and depreciation.

Problems usually surface at the estimate stage. Missed damage, low pricing or a dispute over cause can leave a gap between what the carrier pays and what repairs actually cost. If your claim was denied outright, read what an appraiser can do after a denied insurance claim.

Does a reported loss affect your insurance?

It can. Insurers look at claim frequency and type when they price and underwrite policies. A reported loss may show up on your CLUE report even if the claim was small or closed without payment, and in some cases even an inquiry about a potential claim may be recorded.

That does not mean you should avoid reporting real damage. A valid claim exists to pay for real losses. It does mean you should think carefully about small losses that fall near or below your deductible, and that you should report accurately and completely when you do file.

Also note that we publish a shorter companion piece, what does insurance loss reported mean, if you want a quick summary to share.

Next steps after you report a property loss

Once the loss is reported, your job shifts to documenting the damage and checking the carrier's estimate carefully. If the numbers do not match what it will cost to repair, Texas homeowners and businesses have options, including the appraisal clause found in most property policies.

faqs.q: Does insurance loss reported mean the claim was paid?
faqs.a: No. Insurance loss reported only means the insurer was notified of a loss and recorded it. The claim may later be paid, partially paid, denied or closed without payment. Loss history reports usually show the claim status and any amount paid, so check those details rather than relying on the phrase alone.

faqs.q: Is insurance loss reported on a car bad?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. On a vehicle history report, it means an insurer handled a claim on that car, which could be anything from minor hail dents to major collision damage. Ask the seller for repair records, review the details of the entry and have an independent mechanic inspect the vehicle before you buy it.

faqs.q: How long does a reported loss stay on my record?
faqs.a: Claims in the CLUE database generally remain for about seven years from the date of loss. Insurers may consider that history when they underwrite or price a new policy. You can request your report from LexisNexis to see exactly what is listed and dispute any information that is inaccurate.

faqs.q: Can a denied claim show up as a reported loss?
faqs.a: Yes. A claim that was reported and then denied or closed without payment can still appear on a loss history report, usually with a status showing no payment was made. That is one reason to report accurately and to review your loss history before buying a new policy or selling a home.

faqs.q: How soon should I report a property loss in Texas?
faqs.a: As soon as reasonably possible. Most Texas property policies require prompt notice, and reporting early preserves evidence and starts the insurer's deadlines under the Prompt Payment of Claims Act. For weather claims, there are also time limits on lawsuits and pre-suit notice, so waiting rarely helps.
